name: IFAP syndrome
aliases: ichthyosis follicularis, atrichia and photophobia syndrome

clinicalPearls: Defined by the triad of follicular ichthyosis (non-scaling spiny follicular keratoses), atrichia or severe hypotrichosis, and photophobia
Most cases are X-linked and caused by variants in MBTPS2, the same gene implicated in keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans, giving considerable clinical overlap
The skin shows widespread horny follicular spines resembling a nutmeg-grater texture, with absent or sparse scalp hair, eyebrows and lashes
Photophobia reflects corneal involvement, which may progress to corneal vascularisation and scarring with visual impairment
Severity ranges from relatively isolated skin and eye disease to the extended BRESHECK phenotype with brain, ear, skeletal and other anomalies
Diagnosis is clinical and supported by MBTPS2 molecular testing; skin biopsy shows follicular hyperkeratosis with absent or reduced hair follicles
Management is supportive: emollients and keratolytics, protective lubrication and photoprotection for the eyes, and ophthalmology and genetics input
reference.pathophysiology: IFAP syndrome is usually caused by variants in MBTPS2, which encodes a membrane-bound zinc metalloprotease essential for regulated intramembrane proteolysis of transcription factors controlling cholesterol and lipid homeostasis and the endoplasmic reticulum stress response. Impaired activity disturbs epidermal lipid metabolism and follicular keratinisation, producing spiny follicular hyperkeratosis and failure of normal hair growth. The corneal epithelium is similarly affected, giving photophobia and progressive corneal changes. Because the same gene underlies keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans, the two conditions represent an allelic spectrum.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing follicular hyperkeratosis and reduced or absent follicles
Ophthalmological assessment including slit-lamp examination for corneal changes
Neuroimaging and developmental assessment when extended (BRESHECK) features are suspected
Skeletal survey if bony anomalies are suspected
redFlags: Progressive corneal vascularisation or scarring threatening vision
Neurological regression or developmental delay suggesting the extended phenotype
Failure to thrive or systemic anomalies indicating multisystem BRESHECK involvement
Recurrent skin infection over eroded follicular lesions
reference.prognosis: Isolated cutaneous and ocular disease is compatible with a reasonable prognosis with supportive care, but visual outcome depends on corneal involvement and overall prognosis worsens markedly when severe neurological and systemic anomalies are present.
pitfalls: Not recognising the shared MBTPS2 basis and overlap with keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans
Neglecting ocular surveillance so that treatable corneal disease progresses
Attributing hair loss to a primary alopecia rather than the follicular keratinisation defect
Missing extended multisystem features that alter prognosis and counselling
management: There is no disease-specific therapy, so manage the follicular ichthyosis with regular emollients and topical keratolytics, with oral retinoids offering only limited benefit
Protect the eyes with copious ocular lubricants, tinted lenses for photophobia and specialist treatment of corneal vascularisation and scarring
Support the atrichia with scalp care and cosmetic measures such as wigs, as hair growth cannot be restored
Provide regular ophthalmological surveillance to preserve vision and audiological assessment for hearing loss
In the extended BRESHECK phenotype, manage neurological, skeletal and ear anomalies with developmental and orthopaedic support
Coordinate care through dermatology, ophthalmology, audiology and paediatrics
Offer genetic counselling and carrier and family screening given X-linked inheritance through MBTPS2
